sections.title: The Prophecy Against Tyre
observations: Ezekiel 26 begins with a prophecy against the city of Tyre, a prominent Phoenician city known for its wealth and trade. Tyre had boasted about its strength and security, believing itself invulnerable due to its fortified walls and maritime power.
The prophecy is significant as it reflects God's judgment against pride and arrogance. Tyre's confidence in its own power is challenged by the declaration that God will bring destruction upon it.
This section sets the tone for the chapter, emphasizing the sovereignty of God over nations and cities, and the inevitability of divine judgment.

sections.title: The Siege of Tyre
observations: The chapter details the impending siege of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. This historical event illustrates God's use of foreign powers to execute His judgment.
Ezekiel describes how the city will be attacked, its walls broken down, and its towers demolished. The imagery of destruction serves to highlight the totality of God's judgment against Tyre.
This siege is not just a military action; it is a divine act meant to demonstrate God's authority over all nations.

sections.title: The Aftermath of Destruction
observations: Following the siege, the chapter describes the fate of Tyre. The city will become a desolate place, and its inhabitants will be scattered.

The prophecy also indicates that Tyre will be a place for the spreading of nets, symbolizing its complete desolation and abandonment. This imagery reinforces the idea that what was once a thriving city will be reduced to nothing.
The aftermath serves as a warning to other nations about the consequences of pride and disobedience to God.

importantVerses.commentary: God declares that He is against Tyre, emphasizing His active role in the judgment process. This verse highlights the theme of divine sovereignty.
The declaration that Tyre will be made a bare rock signifies total destruction and abandonment. This verse serves as a stark reminder of the consequences of pride.

questions: What does the prophecy against Tyre reveal about God's character and His attitude towards pride and arrogance?
How does the historical context of Tyre's destruction enhance our understanding of this prophecy?
In what ways can we see parallels between Tyre's fate and the fate of modern nations that turn away from God?
